articles.title: Nomenclature

articles.title: “The Hole”: Poetry Like a Gunshot Wound
articles.abstract: Medicine trains clinicians in a particular silence. Through diagnosis, we medicalize the causes of suffering—contusion, laceration, hemorrhage—as though renaming anguish might contain it, keeping it from spilling out of charts and into our own lives. Operating room and ward become, ironically, fluent in the language of suppression. Yet the horrifically wounded body insists on poetry. It is precisely here, in the rupture between what medicine measures and what human beings experience, that the poem becomes not decoration but necessity. In “The Hole,” poetry does not resolve this rupture or even fix the wound, in this case a gunshot to the patient’s head, another in an epidemic of harm. Instead, it plumbs the unspeakable, not by translating it into medical terminology but exposing the violence of what resists translation. The wound’s gore is first shown from various perspectives: artful (“Picasso”), oddly nostalgic (“meatballs,” “cherry jam”), and clinical (“patch,” “excavate,” “evaluate”). Yet all explanation and description fall short, and in that insufficiency, a strange but sustaining intimacy arises. “This hole was vast./It was no bigger than an eye,” the paradoxical lines at the poem’s emotional core show without telling the profound trauma here; the poem seems to actually bleed in its devastating final lines, “It wouldn’t be filled by dreams/or poetry, my hands or gauze.//It would weep a lifetime/onto the table.” Clinicians may survive such encounters through detachment, but poetry urges us, as dangerously and catastrophically as a gunshot, to be injured by them, bloodstained and awed.

articles.title: Health Care Ownership and Patient Care

articles.title: Clarifications in JAMA Clinical Guidelines Synopsis
articles.abstract: In the JAMA Clinical Guidelines Synopsis titled “Antiviral Therapies for Adults With Mild to Moderate COVID-19 Infection,” published online June 30, 2026, several points were rewritten for clarification. In the third paragraph of the Evidence Base section, the second sentence was revised to “Coadministration of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is contraindicated with certain medications due to risk of serious or fatal toxicity (eg, amiodarone, statins [especially simvastatin and lovastatin], phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors [eg, sildenafil], α-blockers [eg, tamsulosin], or benzodiazepines [eg, triazolam, midazolam]) or strong CYP3A inducers (eg, rifampin, carbamazepine, St John’s wort).” In the fifth paragraph of the Evidence Base section, the last sentence was revised to “Patients who can become pregnant should use contraception during molnupiravir use and for 4 days following the last dose if their partner did not also use molnupiravir. Individuals with a male partner who used molnupiravir should use effective contraception for 3 months after the last dose. Patients who are breastfeeding should consider interrupting breastfeeding and instead pump and discard breast milk during treatment with molnupiravir and for 4 days after the last dose.” In the second paragraph of the Discussion section, an additional sentence was added regarding molnupiravir: “It is currently available in the US only through Emergency Use Authorization, although the authorization will be terminated effective June 29, 2027.” This article was corrected online.

articles.title: Resurgence of Malaria in Ethiopia
articles.abstract: This study examines whether emerging drug and diagnostic resistance variants are contributing to Ethiopia’s malaria resurgence.

articles.title: Intra-Arterial Alteplase After Successful Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke
articles.abstract: To the Editor Dr Renú and colleagues reported that adjunctive intra-arterial alteplase after successful thrombectomy “may improve functional recovery” in large vessel occlusion stroke. The randomized clinical trial provides an important test of a plausible reperfusion strategy, but the report leaves a key issue unresolved—the clinical recovery finding rests on a primary outcome that was changed during the trial.

articles.title: Intra-Arterial Alteplase After Successful Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply As described in the original report, the primary outcome was amended at month 12 to improve clinical relevance and interpretability, considering emerging randomized evidence and the established use of the blinded mRS score assessment. The amendment was implemented on February 10, 2025, after enrollment of 283 patients, of whom 214 had completed or were eligible for 90-day follow-up. No interim analyses had been conducted, and no outcome data by treatment group were available at the time of the amendment; therefore, the change was not informed by accumulating trial results.

articles.title: Review of Prepregnancy Care and Counseling
articles.abstract: To the Editor I appreciate the expanded women’s health learning opportunities provided by the JAMA Network journals under the editorial leadership of Linda Brubaker, MD, MS. The comprehensive Review of prepregnancy care and counseling by Dr Cooper and colleagues will be a valuable resource for clinicians caring for women of reproductive age. I am curious whether the authors recommend preconception screening for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. The US Preventive Services Task Force, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend screening for HCV infection. Curative antiviral treatment for HCV infection is available.

articles.title: Review of Prepregnancy Care and Counseling
articles.abstract: To the Editor In reading the otherwise comprehensive article by Dr Cooper and colleagues on prepregnancy care and counseling, we were surprised by the lack of discussion about testing for iron deficiency. Iron deficiency, the world’s most common micronutrient deficiency, is epidemic in young women. Studies of healthy reproductive-aged female patients report that iron deficiency is present in approximately 38% using a ferritin cutoff of 30 μg/L. Questioning for the most frequent etiology, heavy menstrual bleeding, is often absent, and symptoms are frequently normalized and marginalized. In a high-resource population of primigravid patients without symptoms or anemia, iron deficiency was reported in 21%, 47%, and 84%, respectively, at 15 weeks’, 20 weeks’, and 33 weeks’ gestation, with the strongest predictor of severe iron deficiency (ferritin <15 μg/L) in the third trimester being a ferritin level of less than 60 μg/L at 15 weeks’ gestation. Also, McCarthy et al used the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development to determine that a maternal ferritin level of less than 30 μg/L at 15 weeks’ gestation was associated with statistically and clinically significant decrements in language and motor skills in offspring measured at 2 years. Iron deficiency with and without anemia is associated with disorders that negatively affect patients, such as fatigue, restless legs syndrome, pica, and brain fog. Modeling studies have shown that screening for iron deficiency and treating when identified are cost-effective in reproductive-aged female patients. Screening for iron deficiency prior to pregnancy is now recommended by several societies, including the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics, the European Hematology Association, the American Society of Hematology, and the Haematology in Obstetrics & Women’s Health Collaborative (Australia). Counseling young women considering pregnancy options is an ideal time to screen for iron deficiency given its high incidence and morbidity for both mothers and any future children. Therefore, we agree with the increasing number of society recommendations to screen for iron deficiency in all reproductive-aged female patients and all pregnant patients at presentation, irrespective of the presence or absence of anemia.

articles.title: Review of Prepregnancy Care and Counseling—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank Dr Barbieri and Drs Auerbach and DeLoughery for their comments. With regard to Barbieri’s Letter on HCV screening, the US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation is for adults aged 18 to 79 years. We agree with screening reproductive-aged female patients for HCV, as identification of infection and treatment with direct-acting antiviral medications prior to pregnancy can lead to improved maternal health outcomes and reduced perinatal transmission. Auerbach and DeLoughery describe the case for iron deficiency screening in reproductive-aged female patients well. Screening recommendations for iron deficiency vary between professional organizations, as outlined in their recent narrative review. We were unable to find specific recommendations or robust data in prepregnancy counseling studies to support screening for iron deficiency in individuals seeking pregnancy.

articles.title: Suicide Mortality After Launch of the 988 Lifeline
articles.abstract: To the Editor Dr Patel and colleagues reported that the national launch of the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline was associated with an 11% reduction in adolescent and young adult suicide deaths (4372 fewer than expected). These findings suggest that a phone-based open-access crisis service achieved what the traditional health care system seldom does—population-level reductions in mortality. Missing from the authors’ discussion is the close connection between suicide and substance use disorders, particularly opioid use disorder (OUD). Suicidal ideation is highly prevalent (25%-40%) in OUD, and the distinction between opioid-related risk-taking and suicidality is often clinically ambiguous. In the year after an emergency department visit for nonfatal opioid overdose, survivors experienced 282 excess suicide deaths per 100 000 persons vs a demographically matched general population—an 18-fold increase in risk. National Center for Health Statistics data show that unintentional drug overdose deaths outnumber suicide deaths in the age cohort studied by Patel and colleagues. The authors’ outcome definition excluded unintentional and undetermined-intent drug poisonings (International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision [ICD-10] codes X40-X44 and Y10-Y14), which likely include many unrecognized suicide deaths (more than 20% in one study).

articles.title: Suicide Mortality After Launch of the 988 Lifeline
articles.abstract: To the Editor Dr Patel and colleagues’ recent article provided promising evidence that the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline has been successful at preventing suicide death. Indeed, their results comparing “high-uptake” and “low-uptake” states are consistent with a time-series analysis of pre–988 Lifeline data that found that daily increases in call volume were associated with daily decreases in suicide deaths. However, the precision of Patel and colleagues’ estimates could be enhanced by accounting for between-state heterogeneity in 988 Lifeline implementation and relevant state-level contextual factors.

articles.title: Suicide Mortality After Launch of the 988 Lifeline—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank Dr Herring and Dr Purtle for their thoughtful comments. Our study found that suicide mortality among adolescents and young adults decreased after the national launch of the 988 Lifeline, that declines were largest in states where the 988 Lifeline uptake increased most, and that these patterns withstood prespecified falsification testing—analyses checking whether the same decline appeared in outcomes or periods that the 988 Lifeline could not have affected, which would have signaled a spurious result.

articles.title: Optimizing the Therapeutic Ratio in Prostate Radiation Therapy
articles.abstract: Prostate cancer has long served as a fertile ground for innovation in cancer therapy. Compared with many other malignancies, localized prostate cancer occupies a unique clinical space. Although the incidence of new diagnoses is high, prostate cancer often follows an indolent natural history, resulting in a low risk of prostate cancer–specific mortality. Meanwhile, multiple management strategies exist, including surgery, radiation therapy, and active surveillance, which provide similar disease outcomes in appropriately selected men. As a result, treatment decisions for localized disease must account for not only oncologic outcomes but also preservation of urinary, bowel, and sexual function. Over the past several decades, advances in imaging, risk stratification (including genomics), and treatment delivery have steadily reshaped prostate cancer care with a common goal: in men with early-stage disease who receive local therapy, clinicians and investigators must attempt to optimize the therapeutic ratio by maintaining high rates of cancer control, while minimizing treatment-related morbidity.

articles.title: Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy vs Moderately Hypofractionated IMRT for Prostate Cancer
articles.abstract: This randomized clinical trial assesses whether stereotactic body radiotherapy is superior to moderately hypofractionated intensity-modulated radiation therapy in terms of patient-reported urinary irritative/obstructive and bowel quality of life and disease-free survival in patients with localized intermediate-risk prostate cancer.

articles.title: Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy vs Moderately Hypofractionated IMRT for Localized Intermediate-Risk Prostate Cancer Research Summary
articles.abstract: The objective of this study was to assess whether stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) was superior to moderately hypofractionated intensity-modulated radiation therapy (MH-IMRT) for urinary and bowel quality of life and disease-free survival in patients with localized intermediate-risk prostate cancer.

articles.title: Total Intravenous vs Volatile Inhalational Anesthesia for Major Noncardiac Surgery
articles.abstract: This randomized trial assesses the effect of use of total intravenous anesthesia on days alive and at home 30 days after surgery among older adults undergoing major noncardiac surgery.

articles.title: Total Intravenous vs Volatile Inhalational Anesthesia for Major Noncardiac Surgery Research Summary
articles.abstract: This trial examined whether general anesthesia maintenance with total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) improves patient outcomes compared with volatile-based inhalational anesthesia among adults aged ≥50 years undergoing major elective noncardiac surgery.

articles.title: Patient Information: Nicotine Pouches
articles.abstract: This JAMA Patient Page describes nicotine patch use, the possible harms and side effects, accidental use, and dependence.

articles.title: Nurturing Care for Term Small-for-Gestational-Age Infants
articles.abstract: An estimated 250 million children in low- and middle-income countries are unable to meet key developmental milestones due to biological, psychological, and social risk factors, including maternal and child malnutrition, maternal depression, and inadequate early stimulation opportunities. Without early intervention, these adversities pose threats to longer-term development, including poor adult physical and mental health, lower educational attainment, and low income. Given these complex risks, nutrition inputs alone are unlikely to be sufficient to optimize early childhood development, and bundling with early stimulation and responsive care inputs has been proposed. A robust body of evidence now shows that early stimulation and responsive care interventions in the first 1000 days of life promote early development. However, studies of bundled or integrated early childhood stimulation and nutrition interventions on growth and development outcomes have yielded mixed results, and more investigations are needed.

articles.title: Multidomain Intervention for Growth in Term Small-for-Gestational-Age Infants
articles.abstract: This randomized trial assesses the effect of an integrated intervention package including health, nutrition, early child stimulation, and maternal psychosocial support on weight and weight-for-age z scores among term small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants in a low-resource setting.

articles.title: Multidomain Intervention for Growth in Term Small-for-Gestational-Age Infants Research Summary
articles.abstract: This clinical trial investigated whether an integrated health, nutrition, and early stimulation intervention during infancy improves growth in term small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants.

articles.title: Ulcerative Colitis Management in Adults
articles.abstract: This JAMA Clinical Guidelines Synopsis summarizes the American College of Gastroenterology’s (ACG) 2025 clinical guideline update on management of ulcerative colitis in adults.

articles.title: Ceperognastat in Alzheimer Disease
articles.abstract: Alzheimer disease is defined by the accumulation of extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intraneuronal neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau. For many years, drug development efforts have focused on amyloid-β plaques, culminating in the recent approval of the amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibodies lecanemab and donanemab for the treatment of early-stage Alzheimer disease. In parallel, there has been considerable interest in developing treatments directed at tau tangles, the second pathognomonic lesion of Alzheimer disease.

articles.title: Ceperognastat in Early Symptomatic Alzheimer Disease
articles.abstract: This randomized clinical trial examines the efficacy and safety of the potent oral O-linked N-acetylglucosaminidase inhibitor ceperognastat in early symptomatic Alzheimer disease.

articles.title: Ceperognastat in Early Symptomatic Alzheimer Disease Research Summary
articles.abstract: This study evaluated whether the oral O-linked N-acetylglucosaminidase inhibitor ceperognastat, at doses of 0.75 and 3 mg, compared with placebo, slows clinical progression in patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer disease with low to medium tau levels.
